The fingerprint claim also fails: Fig 26.1's three families are long-context RAG Q&A (context 0.95, latency 0.40), chat (context 0.35, latency 0.90) and batch (lines 46/48), none of which is a short-prompt, latency-sensitive, moderate-quality RAG workload; the closest matrix row for a short prompt is 'High-throughput chat -> decode bandwidth -> continuous batching, KV pool sizing, possibly P/D', not cache + breaker. Step 1 then declares the capstone 'a distinct short-prompt workload -- it is not the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case', which makes Step 0's 'the matrix points to' claim impossible as written. Cache + breaker is the capstone's chosen configuration (Patterns B and C, lines 56-60), reached by the architect's judgment -- not pointed to by any existing row.
evidence: chapter-26.md line 102: 'consults the Sec26.2.1 matrix, which points to the cache + breaker combination'; matrix rows lines 27-37 (10 rows; strategies quoted above -- no 'breaker' anywhere in the table); grep -n 'breaker' chapter-26.md -> lines 9, 58, 60, 62, 81 (none inside the matrix); line 46/48 Fig 26.1 families and scores (RAG Q&A latency 0.40 / context 0.95; chat context 0.35 / latency 0.90); line 104: 'The capstone declares a **distinct short-prompt workload** -- it is *not* the canonical 9.2K-input/1.08-s-prefill case of Ch 4.'
